sections.title: Chapter 1. Introduction
sections.content:
1.1 Research Background

Artificial Intelligence (AI) represents a pivotal shift in the

technological landscape, characterized by advancements in machine

learning, big data, natural language processing, and understanding.

These developments enable software agents to execute tasks with

a  level  of  intelligence  parallel  to human  behavior, marking  a

significant milestone in AI's evolution (Poole & Mackworth, 2010).

While AI's roots extend deep into the history of computer science,

it  is the recent surge  in  technological advancements  that has

illuminated its vast potential, unveiling an array of applications that

span various sectors (Min, 2010). Beyond transforming economic

landscapes through  innovative  solutions, ranging from business

process  optimization  and  increased  operational  efficiency  to

systemic revisions in decision-making processes, AI has catalyzed

the creation of new specialized jobs and fostered technological

innovation, thereby stimulating economic growth (Agrawal et  al.,

2022; Sachs, 2023).

In  2022,  OpenAI  developed  ChatGPT,  accelerating  AI

advancements and capturing global attention by demonstrating its

versatility and seamless integration across diverse fields. In 2023,

the compilers of the Collins Dictionary selected AI as their "Word of

the Year," reflecting its growing influence and importance (BBC,

2023). This recognition aligns with the significant increase in AI

adoption  within  the  business  sector.  Currently, 42%  of  large

organizations  actively deploy  AI,  while an  additional 40%  are

exploring the integration of AI technologies into their operations

(Armonk, 2024; Chui et al., 2018).

The primary scope of AI is to serve as a strategic enabler

across  the  business  value  chain,  including e-business, human

capital  management,  operations,  market  research,  customer

relationship management, accounting and finance, sales, marketing,

and more. The core objective of AI business adoption is to enhance

operational  efficiency by  improving  organizational  performance,

increasing   sales,   minimizing   costs,   automating   customer

management, saving time, and facilitating advanced data collection

and  analysis. According  to the research from Korea SMEs &

Startups Institute (2024), if AI is successfully introduced across all

sectors of the Korean economy,  it  is expected to generate an

overall economic impact of KRW 310 trillion by 2026. An analysis

of the anticipated AI benefits by industry indicates that the service

sector would benefit the most with KRW 136 trillion, followed by

manufacturing  with KRW  77   trillion  and  information  and

communications technology (ICT) with KRW 24 trillion.

In  practice, companies  that have adopted AI  often see

tangible  outcomes. About 40%  reported  early  returns on AI

investment  in the form of increased productivity and improved

customer  experience.  Additional  returns  include new  revenue

streams (27%), faster time to market (30%), improved profitability

(35%), cost savings (35%), market expansion (27%), and more

(PwC, 2024). Reflecting these benefits, a domestic survey by the

Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the Korea Institute

for Industrial Economics and Trade found that 78.4% of firms see

AI adoption as necessary for productivity improvements and cost

reduction. Yet only 30.6% actually deploy AI in practice, indicating

a stark gap between recognized importance and actual usage (Maeil,

2024).

Despite growing interest and adoption, out of the thousands

of companies that have adopted or intend to adopt AI, only 8%

reported  successful  AI  engagement   in  core  practices  and

widespread use. The remainder have limited their efforts to pilot

programs  or  single  business  units  (Fountaine  et   al.,  2019).

Additionally, over 60% of companies planning to adopt AI face

budget  overruns  and  schedule  delays  (Alicke  et   al.,  2021).

Technological inadequacies, scarcity of AI expertise, organizational

resistance  to  change,  security  apprehensions,  and  ambiguity

regarding  viable business cases have  all been  cited as  critical

obstacles to AI adoption (Mishrif & Khan, 2023; Rojas-Berrio et al.,

2022;  Solaimani &  Swaak,  2023).  Companies  often  invest

substantial resources in data infrastructure, AI software tools, and

model development, only  to face disappointment due  to unmet

executive expectations.

Such challenges are particularly evident among Small and

Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs), which typically have limited

capital, a narrower pool  of  skilled  talent, and less established

market presence, factors that can complicate technology adoption

(Akpan et al., 2022; Dong & Yang, 2020; Lee & Xia, 2006; Sanga &

Aziakpono, 2023). The importance of company size in technology

acceptance and adoption has been acknowledged in various studies

(Chatterjee et  al., 2023; Effendi et  al., 2020; Scherer, 1986).

Though SMEs can benefit from less hierarchical decision-making

structures  and  thus more  agile  deployments,  they   still  face

pronounced obstacles in aligning resources, attracting specialized

personnel, and integrating AI across the organization (Dong & Yang,

2020).

In Korea,  this  challenge  is  particularly  salient.  Despite

Korea’s  strong  reputation  for  technological  advancement,  the

country ranks among the lowest  in technology adoption among

OECD  nations  (Park, 2023).  In 2015, the Korean government

initiated the Manufacturing Innovation 3.0 policy, aiming to position

South Korea at the forefront of global manufacturing innovation by

leveraging  smart  factory  technologies.  This  policy  sought  to

enhance  the  competitiveness  of  core  industries  through  the

establishment of 10,000 smart factories and substantial public-

private R&D investments, ultimately propelling South Korea into the

top four global manufacturing nations with a trillion-dollar export

target by 2024 (KDI, 2015). Although the government’s efforts

and  the  success  of  early  adopters  have  demonstrated  clear

efficiencies, the penetration of Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR)

technologies, particularly AI, within the SME sector remains modest.

By 2024, even though top management in manufacturing firms, a

sector with low adoption rates, recognized AI as a crucial lever for

securing competitive advantage, only 16% of SMEs embarking on AI

adoption  reported  successful  integrations  meeting  their  initial

objectives (Lim, 2024).

In response, the government introduced a voucher program

in 2020  to  financially support and  foster connections with AI

solution and providers (NIPA, 2024). The COVID-19 pandemic

further accelerated digital transformation across sectors, pushing

businesses to integrate AI and related 4IR tools more aggressively

(Mishrif & Khan, 2023). Consequently, AI adoption among Korean

SMEs rose from 2.2% in 2019 to 27.8% in 2022 (MSIT, 2020,

2023).

However, the fundamental challenges remain unresolved.

According to the survey shown in Figure 1, the biggest challenges

of AI adoption are “Data Shortage and Data Quality Issues” and

the “Shortage of Skilled Workforce and Hiring Difficulties”. While

both factors slightly decreased in 2023 compared to 2022, they

continue to be significant barriers for many companies. On the other

hand,   certain   challenges   have   intensified,  most   notably

“Insufficient IT Infrastructure to Support AI”, which increased

substantially from 12.9%  in 2022 to 19.9%  in 2023. This rise

suggests that as companies progress in adopting AI, limitations in

their technical infrastructure are becoming more evident. Overall,

while external factors such as legal and ethical concerns remain

minimal, the majority  of  barriers are  internal. Issues such as

workforce shortages, infrastructure limitations, and organizational

readiness  highlight the need for companies to strengthen  their

internal capabilities to effectively implement and scale AI solutions.

Figure 1 Challenges and Barriers of AI Adoption in Korea

Source : ITWorld, 2023

Given these gaps between perceived necessity and actual

adoption success,  it is crucial to investigate which factors most

strongly influence AI adoption. Identifying such determinants can

help businesses and policymakers develop targeted strategies to

overcome existing barriers. In particular, organizational readiness,

encompassing  top management  support, resource  allocation, IT

infrastructure,  and  workforce  capabilities,  appears  pivotal  for

effective AI integration.

1.2. Purpose of the Study

This paper aims to examine the adoption of AI in Korean

SMEs and the factors influencing this process. Despite Korea’s

reputation for technological advancement, the country demonstrates

relatively low adoption rates for new technologies, ranking among

the lowest among OECD countries (Park, 2023). This paradox,

where  significant  technological  progress  coexists  with  limited

utilization,  indicates  the  presence  of  substantial  barriers  that

restrict access  to and  integration  of AI  technologies.  Korea's

distinct technological landscape offers a valuable context to study

AI adoption challenges.

The primary  objective  of  this study  is  to  identify  the

interrelated  dynamics  between  organizational  factors  and  AI

adoption rates among Korean SMEs. Existing research indicates

that organizational factors play a significant role in challenging AI

adoption outcomes. Therefore, this study explores the relationships

between  AI  adoption  rates   in  Korean  SMEs  and  various

organizational factors to identify patterns and associations. Many

studies have previously explored the factors affecting technology

adoption using different research frameworks and Technological-

Organizational-Environmental (TOE) and Diffusion of Innovations

(DOI) are the most commonly used frameworks to evaluate the

innovation adoption. This study will utilize only the organizational

factors and IT innovation readiness factors of both theories to

analyze the internal factors affecting AI adoption (Wisdom et  al.,

2014).  This  blended  approach  allows  for  examination  of  the

complex influences on the adoption of AI in Korean SMEs, providing

a richer understanding of both the internal characteristics and the

contextual factors that promote or inhibit AI adoption.

The study aims to answer important questions about how

organizational readiness affects the adoption and integration of AI

technologies  in these firms. Additionally, the findings from  this

research aim to offer a clearer understanding of the barriers and

facilitators of AI adoption. By analyzing these relationships, the

study seeks to provide valuable insights for businesses, particularly

Korean SMEs, to better prepare for and support AI integration

within their operations.

The study leverages data from a comprehensive survey

conducted by the Korea Technology and Information Promotion

Agency for SMEs (TIPA) in February 2023. The dataset includes

mainly responses from 4,300 SMEs with 300 corporation data for

comparison, providing a comprehensive analysis of the current state

of digital transformation.

This study makes  significant  contributions  to  the  field.

Firstly, this study offers an empirical analysis of AI adoption trends

within Korean SMEs, addressing a gap in existing literature by

focusing on a sector that has been relatively under-explored. By

analyzing  publicly  available survey  data,  this study  delivers a

comprehensive overview  of  the  current  state  of AI  adoption,

offering a valuable reference for understanding this underexplored

sector. Secondly, the study examines the role of organizational

readiness in the adoption process. By focusing on internal factors

such as organizational resources, preparedness, and IT innovation

readiness, the study identifies associations and patterns that help

explain the challenges SMEs face during the adoption process. This

approach contributes to a deeper understanding of the dynamics

within  organizations  that  influence  their  ability  to  adopt  and

integrate AI technologies. Finally, unlike previous studies that rely

heavily on specially designed surveys or small-scale data, this

research leverages publicly available large-scale data. The dataset

allows for a more objective and robust analysis. By doing so, the

study not only highlights key barriers but also identifies enabling

factors that can facilitate smoother AI integration.

In summary, this research bridges the gap between AI’s

technological  potential and  its  practical  application.  It provides

policymakers and business leaders of SMEs with actionable insights

to  better  prepare  and  support  AI  adoption.  By  addressing

organizational readiness, the findings offer guidance on how SMEs

can navigate the digital transformation process and leverage AI to

drive sustainable growth and innovation.

Chapter 2. Data & Method

2.1. Data

The study leverages data from a comprehensive survey

conducted by the Korea Technology and Information Promotion

Agency for SMEs (TIPA) in February 2023. The survey aimed to

measure  the  digital  transformation  landscape,  providing  critical

insights into the readiness for digital transformation and AI adoption

across  a  wide  range  of  organizations. The  dataset  primarily

comprises responses from 4,300 SMEs. Additionally, data from 300

corporations and 300 beneficiary companies were provided  for

comparison purposes. For the analysis, observations from 4,300

SMEs and 300 corporations were utilized. The questionnaire in the

survey not only evaluates the level of digital transformation but also

explores intentions, plans, investments, education, and the use of

ICT technologies, all of which are crucial in influencing AI adoption

or the intention towards it.

To  ensure  data  accuracy  and  reliability,  observations

identified as insincere or inconsistent were excluded. This included

responses lacking financial information, such as capital, revenue, or

profit over the past two years. Contradictory answers were also

eliminated, such as respondents claiming to utilize AI but failing to

specify the type of AI being used. Additionally, responses providing

irrelevant answers, such as indicating “Cash” or “Credit Card” for

business transaction types where options like B2B, B2C, or B2G

were required, were removed.

After the data refinement process, the final dataset included

a  total  of  4,017  observations  compromised  of  3,726 SME

observations and 291 corporation observations for analysis. This

cleaned and  filtered  dataset  provides  a  robust  foundation  for

understanding the factors influencing AI adoption and the digital

transformation readiness of Korean SMEs.

2.2. Measures

Before proceeding with the  analysis,  certain multi-item

questions were refined to construct a new variable. For SMEs,

annual revenue  data were supplemented by matching  financial

statements obtained from corporate information providers, such as

NICE Information Service. In the case of corporations, exact firm

size codes were unavailable, necessitating the establishment of

unifying criteria. To address this limitation, 2021 and 2022 annual

revenue data were  utilized. Given the high correlation between

these two  variables  (corr =  0.996),  their average  value was

calculated for consistency. Based on this average, a stratification

method similar to the original Firm Size Code approach was applied,

with the lower threshold adjusted to start at KRW 1 million, the

minimum observed value  in the  dataset. Table 1 presents the

distribution of firms categorized by revenue range, based on the

newly constructed average annual revenue data.

Table 1 Distribution of Firm Size by Revenue Range

To ensure  consistency  of  the  analysis,  the number  of

regular workers was transformed into a 7-point scale, similar to

the Firm Size  classification. This transformation was based on

Korean labor standards for regular workers. Table 2 displays the

distribution of firms categorized by the number of regular workers

and original Firm Size. A linear relationship is observed between

the number of regular workers and firm size, suggesting that the

application of this standard is valid.

Table 2 Distribution of Firms by Regular Workers and Firm Size

Next,  a  specific  query  posed  is:  "Has  your company

conducted any IT (Information Technology) training sessions for

employees or executives during the past year (from January 2023

to December 2023)? Please check  all that apply." The options

include: i) For employees; ii) For IT Specialists; iii) For executives;

iv) For CEO; v) Did not conduct IT training session. To assess the

degree of IT training, a new variable was constructed, formulated

as a cumulative index of the options.

Another case was  for  Data and  privacy  security. The

specific query is composed of multiple sub-questions to determine

the degree of implementing each security system, which resulted

with hundreds of null data. There were a total of 6 security system

that needed to be answered: 1) Information Asset Identification and

Management Process; 2) Storage Media Management System; 3)

Illegal  Spam  Mail  Blocking  System;  4)  Information  Breach

Prevention  System;  5)  Anti-Virus  and  Malware  System;  6)

Information  Security  Training Program. The sub-query asked

whether the system is needed, being used or planning to adopt

within the next two years. To operationalize this, an ordinal scale

ranging from 1 to 5 was established. 1 - "Not necessary and not

implemented";  2 -  "Not  necessary  but  implemented";  3 -

"Necessary but no plan to implement within the next two years"; 4

- Necessary and planning to implement within the next two years;

5 - "necessary and implemented."

Lastly, for IT and data infrastructure,  it includes multiple

items and each system's degree of usage. It includes mobile office,

cloud service, CRM data, SCM data, and partner data. For mobile

office, a specific query posed is: "Select all types of mobile service

used" and "Are you planning to implement or extend specific mobile

service?"  In  line  with  previous  variable,  Mobile  Office  Data

Infrastructure is constructed as an ordinal scale ranging from 1 to 4.

In this scale, 1 signifies null intention, progressing up to 4, which

represents using the service and planning to extend.

2.3. Descriptive Statistics

Table 3  provides  a summary  of  firms  categorized by

industry, presenting the distribution of SMEs and corporations. The

data shows that while manufacturing comprises a significant portion

of firms at 39.71%, the service sector accounts for the largest

share, representing 47.97% of the total dataset. This reflects the

growing importance of service-related industries  in the Korean

economy. The service sector further demonstrates a  relatively

balanced  distribution  across  various  industries,  highlighting  its

diverse  contributions.  Lastly,  the  construction  sector,  although

smaller in comparison, still represents around 12.32% of the firms,

indicating a moderate level of participation across both SMEs and

corporations.

Table 3 Descriptive Statics of Firms by Industry

One key difference between SMEs and corporations lies in

the representation of the Information and Communication industry.

While the service sector for SMEs appears evenly  distributed,

corporations show a notably higher concentration in this category,

with  13.4%   of   firms  belonging   to   the   Information  and

Communication industry. According to the proportions t-test (p-

value = 0.006), this difference is statistically significant, indicating

that larger firms are more active in technology-intensive industries

leveraging  advanced   technologies  and   investing   in   digital

infrastructure  to  maintain  competitiveness.  Overall,  the  data

highlights a sectoral balance across the dataset, with the service

sector taking the largest share, followed by manufacturing and the

construction  sector.  These  proportions  suggest   that  while

manufacturing remains a key sector in the Korean economy,  it is

not  dominant. This underscores  the importance  of  considering

sectoral  differences  in subsequent analyses  to ensure a more

nuanced understanding of firm-level dynamics.

Table 4 presents the distribution of firms based on average

annual revenue, combining both SMEs and corporations  into a

unified  dataset. As  previously  mentioned,  revenue  data were

averaged from 2021 and 2022 to ensure consistency and address

missing values. The data show that firms are relatively evenly

distributed  across  revenue  categories,  capturing  a  balanced

representation  of  small,  mid-sized,  and  large  firms.  This

comprehensive  distribution ensures the  inclusion  of firms with

varying financial capacities and provides a robust foundation for

analyzing revenue-based firm characteristics and performance.

Table 4 Distribution of Firms by Industry and Revenue Range

AI adoption patterns are detailed in Table 5 and Table 6

Table 5 shows  the  proportion  of  firms  that  report  using  AI,

segmented by SMEs and  corporations. The  proportions t-test

reveals that corporations exhibit a statistically significantly higher

AI adoption  rate than SMEs, suggesting  that  larger firms are

generally more inclined to integrate AI into their operations.

Table 5 Distribution of Firms by Degree of AI Adoption

Table 6 is based on the firms that reported to use AI in prior,

identifying the specific types of AI technologies they employ among

the 263 SMEs and 40 corporations that reported using AI. Because

a  single  firm may employ  multiple AI  types, each percentage

reflects the share of AI-adopting firms within the SME or corporate

group. Manufacturing-related AI shows the highest adoption rate

among SMEs  with 23.19%,  signifying  its  strong  relevance  in

production-oriented environments, and corporations  also report

significant use in this category with 22.50%. However, the data do

not  specify which AI  tools belong  to  “manufacturing-related,”

limiting  further  analysis  of  their precise  applications. IoT and

sensor data analysis emerges as the most prominent category for

corporations with 25.00%, a significantly higher proportion than the

SME rate of 17.87% (p = 0.0025). This suggests that larger firms

place greater emphasis on real-time monitoring and automation,

likely due to more complex operational demands. Another notable

difference appears in customer data analysis and recommendation,

and demand forecasting and financial data analysis. reflecting larger

firms’ tendency to invest more heavily in data-driven decision-

making.

On the other hand, SMEs and corporations both demonstrate

moderate interest in image processing and text analysis, suggesting

that these tools are broadly applicable across various sizes and

sectors. Meanwhile, domain-specific AI remains  least adopted

overall, similar to the manufacturing-related category, the data

does not specify which sub-technologies fall under this label.

In  sum,  SMEs  appear   to   adopt   strongly  toward

manufacturing-focused  AI  solutions,  while  corporations  show

significantly  higher  proportions  in  areas  requiring  substantial

resource investment, such as IoT and sensor-based automation and

data-driven  decision  support. These  patterns  underscore  the

importance of operational complexity and available resources  in

shaping  AI  adoption,  with  statistically  significant  differences

favoring corporations in multiple AI categories.

Table 6 Specifics of AI Utilized by SMEs and Corporations

Together, these tables provide a comprehensive overview of

AI adoption and the specific types of AI technologies utilized by

SMEs and corporations. While corporations lead in AI adoption,

reflecting their greater capacity to integrate advanced technologies,

SMEs are gradually incorporating AI into their operations with a

focus on practical tools such as manufacturing-related AI and IoT

and  sensor  data  analysis.  In  contrast,  more  specialized  AI

categories, like domain-specific AI, remain less utilized across both

groups. These patterns highlight the need for targeted support and

capacity-building initiatives to help SMEs overcome barriers and

fully leverage the benefits of AI.

sections.title: The methodology for this study follows a structured multi-
sections.content:
step  approach  to  ensure  a  rigorous  analysis  of  the  factors

influencing AI adoption and the degree of AI usage among SMEs

and  corporations  (Figure  2).  The   first  step  involves  the

simultaneous definition of the theoretical framework and selection

of survey items. A comprehensive literature review is conducted to

establish the theoretical foundation, which identifies key constructs

and relationships relevant to AI adoption. Based on this framework

and prior studies, survey items are selected from the existing

dataset  to ensure  alignment  with  the research  objectives and

theoretical underpinnings.

The second step focuses on reorganizing the pre-designed

survey  items  into  meaningful  constructs  through  Hierarchical

Clustering Analysis (HCA). Ward’s  criterion  is  applied as the

clustering method due to its recognized accuracy and effectiveness

in  creating  distinct  and  reliable  clusters  (Vinzi,  2010).  This

approach allows the survey items to be grouped empirically in a

manner  that  reflects  their  theoretical  relevance,  providing  a

structured foundation for further analysis.

Third, the Measurement Model Assessment is conducted to

verify the  validity and  reliability of the constructs. Convergent

validity is assessed through factor loadings and average variance

extracted (AVE), while discriminant validity is evaluated using the

Fornell-Larcker  Criterion, Heterotrait-Monotrait (HTMT)  ratio,

and  cross-loadings.  Reliability  is  measured  using  composite

reliability, Cronbach’s alpha, and Rho_A (Putra, 2022). This step

ensures that the re-clustered constructs are both valid and reliable

for analysis.

Fourth,  the  Structural Model Assessment  evaluates  the

relationship  between  the  constructs  and  tests  the  research

hypotheses.  This  includes  examining  collinearity  through  the

Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) and assessing predictive relevance

and effect sizes using R2, f2, and Q2. Path coefficients are analyzed

for  significance  and  relevance  using SmartPLS  4.0  with  the

bootstrapping procedure (Hair Jr et  al., 2014), providing insights

into the strength and direction of the relationships.

Lastly, a path analysis and Multigroup Analysis (MGA) is

sections.title: performed to compare results between SMEs and corporations.
sections.content:
Before conducting the MGA, Measurement Invariance of Composite

Models (MICOM)  is  tested  to  confirm  configural  invariance,

compositional invariance, and the equality of composite means and

variances (Matthews, 2017). Once invariance  is established, the

path  coefficients  are compared  across  the two  groups  using

permutation procedure to identify any significant differences in AI

adoption patterns (Klesel et al., 2019).

approach to analyzing AI adoption by SMEs and corporations. By

integrating a robust theoretical framework, clustering techniques,

measurement   validation,   structural   equation   modeling,  and

multigroup  analysis, the study  effectively repurposes a survey

dataset  not  originally designed  for  this purpose. Through  this

approach, the study successfully and systematically explores the

factors driving AI adoption.

Chapter 3. Research Model & Hypothesis

3.1. Theoretical Framework

sections.title: The  introduction  of new  technologies  inevitably  raises
sections.content:
questions about the factors that influence individuals' decisions to

accept and adopt these innovations. In response to this question,

scholars in various fields have developed a variety of models and

theoretical frameworks aimed at understanding and predicting user

behavior toward technology adoption. These models serve as the

basis for numerous studies, with researchers either using these

established frameworks or integrating and extending them with new

constructs to advance their investigations.

Figure 3 An Overview of Technology Adoption and Acceptance Frameworks and Theories

Source : Taherdoost, 2018

Figure 3  provides a comprehensive diagram of traditional

technology adoption and acceptance frameworks, highlighting the

interdisciplinary roots of these models (Taherdoost, 2018). Among

different frameworks, the Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory and

the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)  focus  primarily on

individual beliefs about technology. These frameworks are often

used in the field of information management, along with the Unified

Theory  of  Acceptance  and  Use  of  Technology  (UTAUT)

(Taherdoost, 2018). Originating from sociology, DOI offers a unique

perspective by  emphasizing  the  technological  factors  that  can

explain and predict adoption decisions. However, it is limited in that

it does not consider the environmental or organizational factors that

can also play a critical role in influencing adoption.

To   address    the    limitation,    the   Technological-

Organizational-Environmental (TOE) framework emerges  as  a

comprehensive   alternative.  By   incorporating   technological,

environmental, and organizational dimensions, the TOE framework

enhances the explanatory power of the DOI with respect to intra-

firm innovation diffusion processes (Hsu et al., 2006). This holistic

approach  allows  for  a  more  in-depth  understanding  of  the

compound influences on technology adoption, positioning the TOE

framework as a  critical  tool  for  analyzing the complexities  of

technology integration within organizations.

The  Diffusion  of  Innovations  (DOI)  theory  (Rogers &

Williams, 1983), examines how the characteristics of a technology

and the perceptions of users influence its adoption. Rogers argues

that the process of innovation diffusion  is essentially a form of

communication that occurs through various channels within a social

system. At the core of DOI are five critical attributes of innovation:

relative  advantage,  compatibility,  complexity,   trialability,  and

observability.  Relative advantage refers to the extent to which an

innovation is perceived as superior to the concept it replaces, which

significantly  influences  its  adoption  (Sharifani  et   al.,  2022).

Compatibility measures how consistent the innovation is with the

existing values, past experiences, and needs of potential adopters.

Innovations that are aligned with the norms and values of individuals

or the social system tend to spread more quickly (Sharifani et al.,

2022). Usually, relative advantage and compatibility has a positive

influence  on  diffusion  of  innovation.  Complexity  denotes  the

perceived  difficulty  of understanding and  using  the  innovation,

typically having a negative effect on its diffusion (Sharifani et al.,

2022). Trialability allows for the innovation to be experimented

with on a limited basis, and observability represents the extent to

which the results of an innovation are visible to others, enhancing

its adoption potential (Sharifani et al., 2022).

These five key attributes significantly impact the rate of

innovation adoption. Together, they account for a substantial portion

of the variance in adoption rates, ranging from 49% to 87% (Ilin et

al., 2017). Beyond the characteristics of the innovations themselves,

organizational   factors  such  as   centralization,   organizational

complexity,    size,    slack    resources,    formalization,   and

interconnectedness also play a crucial role  in the adoption and

utilization of innovations (Hsu et  al., 2006). These organizational

characteristics, along with the innovation characteristics, provide

comprehensive framework for understanding the varying nature of

technology adoption (Tornatzky et al., 1990). Figure 4 (a) visually

shows the impact of characteristics on adoption of innovations.

Figure 4 DOI & TOE Framework

Note. DOI(a) and TOE(b) Framework

Source : Ilin et al., 2017

The    Technology-Organization-Environment    (TOE)

(Tornatzky  et  al., 1990),  describes  the process  of  innovation

adoption in a firm context. This framework, illustrated in Figure 4

(b), identifies three key aspects that influence a firm's decision to

adopt an innovation: technology, organization and environmental

contexts.

The  technology  context encompasses  both  internal and

external technologies  relevant  to the  organization, focusing on

aspects such as technology readiness, complexity, compatibility,

perceived  benefits and  security concerns  (Affia  et  al., 2019;

Janssen et  al., 2020; Lai et  al., 2018; Verma & Bhattacharyya,

2017; Yadegaridehkordi et al., 2018). This dimension assesses the

availability and  characteristics  of  technologies  that  are  either

currently in use or not yet adopted by the organization and shapes

the scope and limits of potential technological change. Technologies

in use influence adoption decisions by determining the extent of

technological change the firm is willing to undertake, while those

not in use highlight opportunities for evolution through the adoption

of new  technologies.  These  external  technologies  can  drive

incremental,  synthetic  or  discontinuous  change,  with  different

degrees of risk associated with each type (Baker, 2012)

The organizational context is concerned with the inherent

characteristics  of  the  organization,  the  resources  and  the

communication processes among individuals. Key elements within

this context  include  organizational  culture, change management

strategies, vision and strategy alignment, available resources and

competencies, and most importantly, top management commitment

and support (Alreemy et al., 2016; Duan et al., 2017; Hentschel et

al., 2019; Lai et al., 2018, p. 4; Nah & Delgado, 2006; Ramamurthy

et  al., 2008). Organizational characteristics significantly influence

the adoption and implementation process, where the organizational

structure, communication protocols and managerial behavior can

either facilitate or hinder innovation adoption.

Lastly,  the  environmental  context  reflects  the  industry

structure,  technological  support  infrastructure  and  prevailing

government regulations. It also includes factors such as institutional

trust,  demand   volatility,  competitive  pressures  and   ethical

considerations  (Bahmanziari  et   al.,  2003; Duan  et   al.,  2017;

Hasibuan & Dantes, 2012; Lai et  al., 2018; Nguyen, 2013). All

these factors contribute to the external pressures and opportunities

that influence an organization’s innovation adoption decisions.

Although the TOE framework is widely used, recent studies

have  extended  its  scope by  integrating   it  with  the Human-

Organization-Technology  fit model (HOT), thus adding a human

dimension to the traditional framework (TOEH) (Dora et al., 2022;

Kumar et  al., 2023; Yadav et  al., 2023; Yang et  al., 2013). This

extension allows for a more comprehensive analysis of the role that

employees play  in the innovation adoption  decision, addressing

aspects such as employee competence,  training, and  effective

communication with partners that were previously overlooked in the

traditional framework (Nilashi et al., 2016; Orji et al., 2020).

The TOE framework and DOI theory  exhibit  significant

overlap, particularly in the domains of innovation characteristics and

the technological context, as well as organizational characteristics

and the organizational context. This alignment underscores their

complementary  perspectives  in  examining  factors  influencing

innovation adoption. In TOEH framework, organizational context is

more specified as organizational and human context. Moreover, TOE

framework does not consider  specifics such as  trialability and

observability, and DOI  theory does  not  include  environmental

factors.  Therefore,   integrating  these  two  frameworks  can

strengthen the overall  analysis. The integration of Diffusion of

Innovations (DOI) theory with the TOE framework has proven to be

a robust approach for studying the adoption of Fourth Industrial

Revolution (4IR) enablers, such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and

cloud computing. Studies have demonstrated the usefulness of this

combined DOI-TOE model in identifying the factors influencing the

adoption of these technologies, highlighting its applicability across

different 4IR technologies (Dash & Anusandhan, 2018; Olushola,

2019).

Nevertheless, when each factor is considered in isolation, it

is  plausible  that some  factors may  influence  others,  thereby

suggesting the potential presence of causal relationships among

them.  It  is therefore not  logical to examine these elements  in

isolation. To address this limitation, a study has proposed a model

that integrates IT Innovation Readiness factors such as Technology

Readiness and  Internal Expertise as mediating variables  in the

relationship between organizational factors and technology adoption

(Ali  et   al.,  2022).  This  model  is  adopted  from  Context-

Mechanism-Outcome (CMO) perspective, which is broad enough to

be applicable within a general context that can measure differential

organizational effects (Wisdom et al., 2014). Organizational factors

represent the context that influences organizational strategy and

subsequent adoption of the innovative IT as the final outcome. The

organizational factors included in this model are Top Management

Support, Organizational Structure and Organizational Culture. While

the original framework focused on general IT innovation adoption,

this paper will specifically examine AI adoption within Korean SMEs.

Figure 5 CMO Framework of Organizational Factors in IT Adoption

Source: Ali et al., 2022

3.2.1. Organizational Factors

Organizational  factors  were  examined  through  three

constructs based on the CMO framework: Top Management Support,

Organizational Culture, and Organizational Structure.

It has been  definitively evidenced  that the  role  of top

management   in   facilitating  the  implementation  of  innovative

technology is of the utmost importance. Their support is vital for

the allocation of resources, the fostering of an organizational culture

that embraces innovation, and the steering of the strategic vision

that integrates technology as a key component of the organization’s

growth (Jöhnk et  al., 2021). A review of the literature on the

adoption  of  innovative  technologies  consistently  identifies  top

management  support  (TMS)  as  a  critical  factor  influencing

technology adoption (Hsu et al., 2006; Kumar Bhardwaj et al., 2021;

Lian et al., 2014; Oliveira et al., 2014). TMS encompasses factors

such as the top management's interest, knowledge, and willingness

to adopt innovative technologies, as well as their role and intention

in investment planning and strategy development.

Organizational culture plays a pivotal role in the adoption of

innovative technologies. It not only influences the intention to adopt

such technologies but also shapes how organizations integrate and

utilize them (Kuusisto, 2017). A key dimension of organizational

culture  is  employee  interest  and  capability,  which  are  often

highlighted as  critical factors  in determining the success of AI

adoption. These aspects  reflect the  effort employees invest  in

learning and effectively utilizing new technologies (Eze et al., 2019;

Sharma et  al., 2022). For SMEs, resource constraints make this

aspect even more critical, as limited human resources often lead to

additional  financial burdens, such as hiring external consultants

(Maduku et  al., 2016). In this context,  it becomes essential for

employees   to  possess  a  basic  awareness  and   functional

understanding  of the IT technologies  their  organization adopts.

While expertise is not necessary, employees must be sufficiently

capable of engaging with the technology to facilitate the integration

into  organizational  processes.  Furthermore,  a  positive  attitude

toward emerging  technologies enables employees  to be  better

prepared  for  the  adoption process  (Siren & Knudsen, 2017).

Another  cultural element  critical  to technology adoption  is the

collective  attitude of employees toward innovation and change.

Organizational culture directly impacts employees’ willingness to

embrace new technologies and their openness to innovative change.

This  study  emphasizes   specific  technology-related   cultural

elements, such  as  user  attitudes toward  innovation and  their

readiness to adapt to technological advancements. These factors

are instrumental in determining the overall success of technology

integration within an organization.

When measuring the organization structure factor, traditional

considerations include key aspects such as organization size and

managerial  structure,  including  centralization  (Damanpour &

Gopalakrishnan, 1998). Size is a crucial component of organizational

structure, as larger companies generally have more resources and

stronger incentives to adopt innovative technologies (Oliveira et al.,

2014).  Although  this  study  focuses on SMEs  in  Korea,  the

difference in revenue stream within the SMEs and the number of

regular employees could be measured to distinguish the firm size

within  SMEs.  Managerial  structure,  including  the  degree  of

centralization and formalization, is widely recognized as a critical

factor influencing technology adoption. Research suggests that a

highly decentralized structure can enhance product visibility and

foster a collaborative environment by enabling multiple tasks to be

processed in parallel (Grant et al., 2021). Decentralization, which

involves  shifting responsibility and authority to lower levels of

management,  often  promotes  greater  collaboration  and  more

positive attitudes toward adopting innovative technologies. However,

some studies, such as those by Moch and Morse (1977) and Wang

and Feeney (2016), have found that managerial structure does not

significantly influence technology adoption, highlighting variability in

its impact across different contexts.

3.2.2. IT Innovation Readiness Factors

For  IT  innovation  readiness  factors,  based  on CMO

framework, two constructs are defined: Technology Readiness and

Internal Readiness. In addition, security is also included as  it is

inevitably  the  most  important  factor  to  consider  in  today's

technology.

Technological  readiness   to  adopt  new   technologies,

especially  AI,  is  critical. This readiness  is determined by the

existing technology infrastructure, compatibility with AI, and the

overall technology strategy that aligns with AI implementation goals.

The success of AI adoption depends heavily on the organization’s

ability to integrate these technologies into its existing systems and

processes (Jöhnk et  al., 2021). Technology readiness facilitates

this integration by ensuring that the necessary infrastructure and

support systems are in place, thereby increasing the likelihood of

adopting AI  technologies  with  organizational needs. Thus,  this

factor includes aspects such as organization's existing technology

resources, along with IT and data infrastructure (Ali & Soar, 2018;

Fu & Chang, 2016).

The presence of a skilled labor force within an organization

is invaluable as they reduce the need for extensive training  in

innovative technologies. This aspect differs from overall human

capital  resource  (HCR)   held   at  the   organizational   level.

Organizational-level HCR is an aggregate of individual-level skills.

On the other hand, the IT experts implement new technology and

help in imparting their expertise to others (Murray, 2018). This

factor will measure the existence of IT specialists as well as data

analysts along with the extent of training held upon employees and

top managers. Training has a direct impact on the organization’s

ability to use AI technologies effectively (Kelley, 2022). Training

programs not only equip employees with the necessary skills, but

also foster an environment of continuous learning and adaptability,

which is critical for navigating the complexities of AI (Ghaleb et al.,

2021).

A  security  breach,  defined  as  an  incident  where  an

organization loses personal records or other sensitive data, poses

significant risks to the company. This risk heightens especially in

the  context  of  AI  as   it  processes  vast  amount  of  data

(MalwareBytes,  2023). The  absence  of  robust  cybersecurity

measures, such as malware protection or secure data storage, can

expose systems to malicious actors, potentially leading to serious

data breaches. Without the existence of proper security for data and

privacy, adopting innovative technology could lead to bigger harm

for the company(Zhu et al., 2006). This aspect includes the degree

of privacy and security of a firm and the maintenance of data

security within the company (Heimberger et al., 2024).

3.3.1. Formulating Constructs using HCA

As  this study  utilizes a pre-designed survey  originally

developed for purposes other than this analysis,  it is crucial to

ensure that the survey items are empirically grouped in a manner

that aligns with theoretical relevance. To achieve this, Hierarchical

Clustering Analysis (HCA) is applied to systematically re-group

the items. The Ward’s  criterion  is employed as the clustering

method, as  it  is renowned  for  its  effectiveness  in  minimizing

within-cluster variance and ensuring high accuracy  in forming

distinct  and  meaningful  clusters  (Vinzi,  2010).  This  method

evaluates potential groupings by minimizing the increase in total

within-cluster  variance, making   it  particularly  well-suited  for

identifying  clear  and  interpretable  clusters  from  pre-existing

survey data.

Figure 6 Hierarchical Clustering Analysis Dendrogram

The dendrogram generated through this analysis, as shown

in Figure 6, illustrates the clustering structure of the survey items

based on  their  similarities. The  labels  represent  the  survey

questions, and the horizontal axis indicates the distances at which

clusters are merged. A cutoff threshold of 1.0 was applied to the

dendrogram to define the clusters systematically, resulting in a set

of  distinct  groups. Each  group  reflects  theoretically  relevant

categorizations of the survey items. These empirically determined

groups are summarized in Table 7, providing a detailed breakdown

of the survey items within each cluster.

Table 7 Summary of Survey Item Clusters Derived from HCA

Using these clusters, the constructs were carefully defined

to ensure they accurately capture the intended dimensions of the

theoretical framework. This process ensures that the constructs are

both empirically grounded and theoretically consistent, facilitating

robust  analysis and  interpretation  in subsequent stages  of the

research. In defining the constructs, variables from the clusters that

appeared to lack theoretical or contextual relevance were excluded

to  maintain  the  focus  and  coherence  of  the  analysis.  This

refinement process ensures that only variables strongly aligned

with the intended constructs are  included. A summary  of the

3.3.2. Construct Definition and Hypotheses

Based on HCA result, each construct is defined as follow and

hypothesized. Figure 7 provides a comprehensive overview of the

hypothesized relationships between the constructs discussed in this

study.

Organization Interest

Organization Interest emphasizes the alignment and unified

commitment  between  top management  and  employees  toward

achieving  digital transformation  goals. This construct integrates

Top  Management  Support  (TMS)  and  Employee  Attitudes,

reflecting their collective role in driving technological adoption and

organizational transformation. The integration of these variables is

supported by their high internal cohesion and minimal variance, as

indicated by the clustering results. Prior research also highlights

that the alignment of top management and employees significantly

influences the success of organizational initiatives (Li et al., 2017),

Technology   Readiness   and   Internal   Readiness   are

collectively influenced by the alignment between top management

and employees, which fosters an environment conducive to adopting

and integrating innovative technologies. Leadership plays a pivotal

role  by  prioritizing  resource  allocation,  strategic  vision,  and

investment planning, while simultaneously fostering a culture of

innovation (Hsu et  al., 2006; Jöhnk et  al., 2021). This alignment

enables the development of necessary infrastructure, the provision

of  training,  and  data management,  which  collectively  address

barriers such as resource constraints and resistance to change

(Maduku  et  al., 2016). Employee  readiness,  reflected  in  their

willingness and ability to adapt, complements leadership efforts by

enhancing operational efficiency and ensuring minimal disruption

during implementation. This synergy ensures that organizations are

equipped with both the technical and cultural readiness needed for

successful digital transformation (Kuusisto, 2017)

Furthermore, the collaboration between top management and

employees  significantly  enhances  an  organization’s  ability  to

proactively address security risks and integrate robust protective

measures. Leadership plays a key role in prioritizing cybersecurity

through strategic planning and investment in security infrastructure

(Poehlmann et al., 2021). Simultaneously, employees contribute by

adopting secure practices and fostering a culture of awareness,

collectively    mitigating    vulnerabilities   and    strengthening

organizational security (Kollarova et  al., 2023). his shared focus

ensures that security measures are seamlessly embedded into the

organization’s digital transformation strategy. For these reasons,

the following hypotheses are defined:

H1a.    OrganizationInterest willpositively affect Technological

Readiness

H1b.    OrganizationInterest willpositively affect Internal

Readiness

H1c.    OrganizationInterest willpositively affect Security

Organization Size

Size is a crucial factor in shaping an organization’s readiness

for  digital transformation. Defined by a firm’s revenue and the

number of regular employees, organizational size often determines

the  availability  of  resources  and  the  capacity  to  implement

innovative technologies (Oliveira et  al., 2014). While this study

focuses on SMEs in Korea, the variation in revenue streams and

workforce size within SMEs provides an additional dimension to

understanding the influence of size on organizational readiness.

Larger  firms  within  the SME category tend  to have  stronger

incentives and more robust capacities for adopting new technologies,

driven by greater  financial  stability and a  larger workforce to

support implementation efforts.

The size of an organization directly impacts Technological

Readiness by  enabling access  to  better  infrastructure,  training

programs, and technological investments. Firms with higher revenue

and larger workforces are better equipped to allocate resources

effectively and overcome barriers to technology adoption (Ali et al.,

2022). Similarly, Internal Readiness is influenced by size, as larger

firms often have more structured processes, better organizational

infrastructure, and the capacity to manage change with greater

efficiency (Ali et al., 2022). Finally, Security readiness is enhanced

in  larger  firms  due  to  their  ability  to  invest  in  advanced

cybersecurity measures and foster a culture of awareness among

employees, mitigating vulnerabilities and protecting digital assets

(Kollarova et al., 2023; Poehlmann et al., 2021). For these reasons,

the following hypotheses are defined:

H2a.    Organization Size will positively affectTechnological

Readiness

H2b.    Organization Size will positively affect Internal Readiness

H2c.    Organization Size will positively affect Security

Technology Readiness

Technology Readiness  refers  to  the degree  of  existing

technology  infrastructure  and  resources  that  align  with  an

organization’s   digital   transformation   goals.   This   construct

emphasizes the importance of having the necessary infrastructure,

compatibility, and strategy  in place  to support the adoption of

advanced  technologies  such  as   artificial   intelligence   (AI).

Technological readiness  is a  critical  factor  in determining  the

success  of AI adoption, as  it ensures  that the organization  is

capable of integrating new technologies seamlessly into its existing

systems and processes (Jöhnk et al., 2021).

The readiness to adopt AI technologies is shaped by the

organization’s existing technology resources, IT systems, and data

infrastructure. Compatibility with AI and a well-defined technology

strategy  further  facilitate  the  integration  process,  minimizing

disruptions and  aligning technology adoption with organizational

goals (Ali & Soar, 2018; Fu & Chang, 2016). Organizations with

robust technological readiness are better positioned to deploy AI

solutions effectively, increasing the likelihood of achieving strategic

objectives through digital transformation. For these reasons, the

following hypotheses are defined:

H3.   Technology Readinesswillpositively affect AI Adoption

Internal Readiness

Internal Readiness refers to the degree of data readiness,

the presence of a skilled labor force, and the availability of IT

training programs within an organization. These factors collectively

determine an organization’s ability to adopt and integrate advanced

technologies like AI. A skilled labor force is critical in reducing the

need for extensive training, as IT specialists and data analysts play

a central role in implementing new technologies and imparting their

expertise to others (Murray, 2018)This readiness extends beyond

the aggregate human capital resources (HCR) of an organization by

emphasizing the specific capabilities of IT professionals who enable

the smooth adoption of innovative technologies.

Training programs are another key component of internal

readiness. These programs equip employees and top managers with

the skills necessary to effectively utilize AI technologies, fostering

an environment of continuous learning and adaptability (Kelley,

2022) By  enhancing  technical  competencies,  training  directly

impacts  an  organization’s  ability  to  navigate  the  complexities

associated with AI adoption (Ghaleb et  al., 2021). Together, the

availability of skilled personnel and robust training initiatives ensure

that organizations are well-prepared to integrate AI  into  their

workflows, minimizing disruptions and maximizing efficiency. For

these reasons, the following hypotheses are defined:

H4.    Internal Readinesswillpositively affect AIAdoption

Security

Security  refers  to  the  degree  of  robust  cybersecurity

measures, such as malware protection, secure data storage, and

privacy protocols, that organizations implement to safeguard their

digital assets. Although the original framework did not explicitly

include security as a factor for IT innovation readiness, it is now

widely recognized as an indispensable component in the context of

emerging technologies. A security breach—defined as an incident

where sensitive data or personal records are compromised—poses

significant risks to an organization, particularly in the adoption of AI,

which processes vast amounts of sensitive data (MalwareBytes,

2023). The absence  of  adequate  cybersecurity measures can

expose systems  to  malicious  actors,  resulting  in severe  data

breaches and potential reputational and financial harm.

Security encompasses not only the degree of privacy and

data protection but also the maintenance of hardware, software, and

networks.  Without  proper  security  protocols,  the  adoption  of

innovative  technologies  such  as AI  could  lead  to  detrimental

consequences, undermining  organizational success. Research by

Heimberger et  al (2024). further emphasizes that security  is a

critical  driving  factor  in AI  adoption, as  robust  cybersecurity

systems enhance  trust and  reliability, which are  essential  for

successful implementation. By ensuring the protection of  digital

assets, organizations can reduce risks and foster an environment

conducive to leveraging AI for strategic advantages. For these

reasons, the following hypotheses are defined:

H5.    Internal Readinesswillpositively affect AIAdoption

Degree of AI Adoption as Dependent Variable

The dependent variable is the degree of AI usage, which is

measured on an ordinal scale from 1 to 5. The scale ranges from

firms with no data collection (1) to those making full use of data/AI

for real-time decisions (5). This classification provides a nuanced

understanding of AI integration within firms, capturing incremental

stages of AI adoption and utilization.

Variables of Control: Manufacturing

Each dataset is coded according to the industry code that is

assigned. Each industry is then categorized according to the sector,

manufacturing or non-manufacturing. By controlling the sector, the

effects specific to manufacturing industries can be isolated. This

ensures that any observed differences in outcomes are attributable

to the variables of interest rather than the inherent characteristics

of the sector (Arroyabe et al., 2024)

4.1. Measurement Model Assessment

To evaluate the proposed model, a measurement model

assessment was conducted. Initially, Principal Component Analysis

(PCA) was performed to identify the final factors and use only

items that strongly represent intended factor, improving overall

reliability and clarity of the final measurement model. Since multi-

group analysis (MGA) will be conducted later, only factors that

satisfy the models based on the complete dataset, SME dataset, and

corporation dataset are used to ensure configural invariance later.

Based on this process, the final factors were selected and shown in

Table 9. Note that Organization Size and Security is a single-item

constructs. Normally, single-item constructs are not preferred as

they may pose challenges to the criterion  validity. However, a

global single item  that effectively captures the essence of the

construct  under  consideration   is  generally  sufficient  as  an

alternative measure in PLS-SEM (Hair Jr et al., 2021).

The structural model was evaluated to confirm its predictive

validity and  stability by examining  multicollinearity, explanatory

power, predictive relevance, and effect sizes. All Variance Inflation

Next, we evaluated the model’s ability to explain and predict

outcomes by examining R-squared (R2), Q-squared (Q2), and the

endogenous variable is explained by its predictors, while Q2 and

4.3. Measurement Invariance of Composite (MICOM)

Before  conducting  the  path  analysis,  the  Multi-Group

Invariance  of  Measurement  Model  (MICOM)  procedure  was

performed to determine whether path comparison across groups

was valid. The analysis was conducted in three steps: Configural

Invariance, Compositional Invariance, and Equality of Composite’s

Mean Value and Variance Across Groups (Matthews, 2017). From

the outset, it was assumed that Step 1, Configural Invariance, was

satisfied, as identical indicators, data treatment procedures, and

algorithm settings were consistently applied across all groups. This

assumption allowed for a smooth progression into subsequent steps

of the MICOM procedure.

In Step 2, Compositional Invariance, the composite scores

for constructs were tested shown in Table 16. This was done by

comparing the "Original Correlation" of the composite scores with

the 5%  quantile  of  the  permutation  distribution.  Compositional

invariance was established  if the original correlation was greater

than or equal to the 5% quantile, or if the p-value was insignificant.

The results confirmed compositional invariance for all constructs,

indicating consistent measurement properties across groups.

Table 16 Results of Compositional Invariance Testing (Step 2)

In Step 3, Equality of Composite’s Mean Value and Variance

Across Groups, the composite's mean and variance differences

were examined presented in Table 17. Full invariance was defined

as both mean and variance differences falling within the 2.5% to

97.5% boundaries, while partial invariance was achieved  if either

the mean or variance alone  fell  within these  boundaries. The

analysis revealed partial invariance for the constructs, as none or

only the variance differences were within the acceptable boundaries

for most constructs.

The MGA  reveals  contrasting  effects  of  Technological

Readiness on AI adoption between SMEs and corporations. In SMEs,

Technological Readiness has a slightly positive relationship with AI

adoption (β = 0.052, p < 0.001), while in corporations, it exhibits a

negative effect (β = -0.107, p < 0.05). a finding that contrasts with

existing literature. This result is possibly due to the construct of

the  measure.  Current  measures  of  Technological  Readiness

primarily focus on  traditional  infrastructure, such as hardware,

software,  and  network  management.   It  is  known  that  more

specialized AI adoption and solution increasingly relies on flexible

and scalable resources, such as cloud-based solutions and high-

performance computing (Campos Zabala, 2023). Moreover, a larger

proportion  of corporations adopt  AI, and many  of these firms

employ more complex  applications  like IoT and  Sensor  Data

Analysis, which require specialized infrastructure including edge

computing, real-time data processing, and scalable cloud services.

This  mismatch  between  the  advanced  requirements  of  these

applications and the traditional focus of Technological Readiness

measures may contribute to the observed negative relationship in

corporations. Overall, these findings underscore the importance of

considering  both  organizational  context  and  the  specific  AI

applications  in use when  interpreting  the  relationship between

Technological Readiness and AI adoption.

Internal  Readiness emerges  as  a  universally  significant

factor across both SMEs and corporations but has a substantially

stronger impact on AI adoption in SMEs (β = 0.715, p < 0.001)

0.193  (p <  0.001). These  findings  underscore  the  universal

importance of Internal Readiness  in enabling AI adoption while

highlighting its elevated influence in smaller organizational contexts.

The findings indicate that data availability and data sharing are

common areas of focus across all organizations, with many working

to improve transparency and integration  in their data collection

processes. Studies have highlighted that creating an ecosystem that

capitalizes on stored data could increase the likelihood of achieving

a higher degree of AI adoption (Felemban et al., 2024). However,

many companies, despite making progress, are still not fully mature

in how they manage and leverage their data. For SMEs, fostering a

robust data-sharing ecosystem could further amplify their ability to

adopt and integrate AI technologies as seen from the result. Their

operational  agility and streamlined  structures  position them  to

maximize  the  benefits  of  Internal  Readiness,  particularly  in

enhancing data-sharing capabilities. These results underline that

while Internal Readiness has a critical impact on the degree of AI

adoption across all organizational types, SMEs stand to gain more

by   prioritizing  transparency  and   integration   in   their  data

ecosystems to have higher degree of AI implementation.

4.5. Mediated Effect Test and MGA Comparison

To examine the role of IT Innovation Readiness factors as a

mediator between  Organizational Factors and AI Adoption, the

mediated effect was analyzed (Hair Jr et al., 2017). Then to analyze

the mediator model, each mediation is categorized into five types

based on the significance and coefficient direction of the direct and

indirect  paths;  indirect-only   (full  mediation),  complementary

(partial mediation), competitive (partial mediation), direct only (no

mediation) and no effect (no mediation) (Zhao et al., 2010). Lastly,

to compare the mediation patterns across different organizational

contexts, MGA was conducted to evaluate whether the mediation

effects differ significantly between SMEs and corporations.

finding underscores the key role of Internal Readiness in facilitating

the translation of Organizational Interest into practical outcomes

that support AI adoption. Specifically, this mediation underscores

the importance of fostering a robust data ecosystem to capitalize

data to achieve successful AI adoption.

sections.title: 5.1. Conclusion
sections.content:
This study examined the factors associated with AI adoption

in Korean SMEs, focusing on  organizational and IT  innovation

readiness  factors  identified through a comprehensive  literature

review and empirical analysis. By incorporating constructs such as

Organizational Interest, Organizational Size, Technology Readiness,

Internal Readiness, and Security, the research provides insights into

the various dimensions that relate to an organization's ability to

adopt AI technologies.

The  findings suggest  that  Organizational  Interest, which

encompasses the alignment and commitment of top management

support and employees’ interest, is strongly linked to IT innovation

readiness, including dimensions such as Internal Readiness and

Security.  Internal  Readiness,  which  involves  factors  like  data

management and  sharing, appeared as an  important dimension

related to AI adoption, highlighting the significance of equipping

organizations  with  the  resources and  practices  necessary  for

technological integration. The inclusion of Security as a construct

emphasizes the role of robust cybersecurity measures in supporting

the adoption of data intensive technologies such as AI.

5.2. Theoretical Implications

This study reinforces the pivotal role of Internal Readiness

as  a  foundational  factor  in  AI  adoption,  demonstrating   its

significance across organizations of varying sizes and resource

levels. By extending the application of the Context-Mechanism-

Outcome (CMO) framework, the research highlights how Internal

Readiness serves as a critical enabler for successful AI integration.

This approach addresses the  limitation of examining factors  in

isolation by integrating IT Innovation Readiness factors, such as

Technology  Readiness,  Internal  Readiness  and  Security,  as

mediating variables between organizational factors and AI adoption

(Ali et al., 2022). Moreover, the inclusion of Security as a construct

marks a significant advancement over existing models, recognizing

its critical role in mitigating risks associated with AI adoption and

providing a more comprehensive understanding of the determinants

of AI integration.

Additionally,  the  comparison between SMEs and  larger

corporations through Multigroup Analysis (MGA) provide deeper

theoretical insights into the differentiated pathways of AI adoption.

The Mediated  Effect Test  reveals  that  Organizational  Interest

significantly influences AI adoption through IT Innovation Readiness

factors, particularly Internal Readiness, more so in SMEs than in

corporations. This mediated relationship suggests that, even in the

presence of resource and financial constraints, effective internal

data management and data integration systems may be associated

with successful AI adoption in SMEs.

5.3. Practical Implications

The findings offer actionable insights for business leaders of

SMEs and policymakers aiming to enhance AI adoption in SMEs.

5.3.1. For Business Leaders in SMEs

For business leaders in SMEs seeking to integrate AI into

their business model, strengthening Internal Readiness is crucial.

Business  leaders  in SMEs  seeking  to  integrate AI  into  their

business model should focus on investing in developing robust data

management  practices and  creating systematic  data  integration

among business partners. Strengthening these internal capabilities

can mitigate resource constraints and enhance the organization's

ability  to  integrate  AI  technologies  effectively.  Additionally,

cultivating a  culture  of continuous  learning and  innovation can

support the seamless adoption and utilization of AI technologies.

5.3.2. For Policymakers

To   effectively  promote  AI  adoption  among  SMEs,

government   initiatives   should   prioritize   providing   financial

incentives  and  support  programs  that  enhance  both  internal

readiness and security measures. Expanding existing AI voucher

programs  to  include  targeted  assistance   for   training  and

cybersecurity can help mitigate the financial and technical barriers

that  SMEs  often   face.   Additionally,  fostering  sector-wide

collaboration   through   shared   investment   mechanisms   or

partnerships can alleviate the substantial  initial costs associated

with  implementing  AI  technologies.  Programs  that   facilitate

knowledge sharing and cooperation between SMEs and AI solution

providers  will  not  only  strengthen  internal  readiness  but  also

improve  the  overall  success  rate  of  AI  implementations. By

addressing resource constraints and encouraging broader industry

coordination,  policymakers  can   create  a  more   supportive

environment that enables SMEs to adopt AI technologies more

effectively and sustainably.

5.4. Limitations and Future Studies

Despite  its valuable contributions, this study has several

limitations. Firstly, the reliance on data from Korean SMEs may

restrict the generalizability of the findings to SMEs operating in

different cultural or economic environments. To address this, future

research should incorporate a more diverse range of SMEs from

sections.title: various  countries  to  validate and expand upon  these  results.
sections.content:
Additionally,  the  dataset used was  not  originally designed  for

studying AI adoption, necessitating adaptations in  its application.

sections.content:
constraints, this factor might still influence the outcomes and should

be considered when interpreting the findings.

Furthermore, the measurement of organizational size was

limited to workforce  size, potentially neglecting other important

aspects such as market influence and revenue size. Future studies

could benefit from including a wider array of indicators to more

accurately capture the multifaceted nature of organizational capacity.

Moreover, due to data  limitations, top management support and

employee behavior were combined into a single construct, which

may compromise construct  validity. Subsequent research should

aim to measure these constructs separately to provide a more

precise evaluation of their individual impacts on AI adoption.

Lastly, this research primarily focused on internal factors

influencing AI adoption, with limited exploration of external factors

like  industry  competition,  regulatory environments, and market

dynamics. Integrating these external variables in future research

could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the drivers

and barriers to AI adoption. Lastly, adopting a longitudinal research

design would  allow  for  the examination  of how  organizational

readiness and AI  adoption  evolve  over  time,  offering  deeper

insights into the dynamic interplay between these factors.

This study examined the relationships between constructs

using  structural equation modeling. While  this approach helped

identify associations,  it does not establish causality. Additionally,

the study did not explore synergistic effects or make comparisons

between constructs. Therefore, future research is recommended to

utilize methods such as Partial Least Squares - Artificial Neural

Networks (PLS-ANN)  to  investigate  causal  relationships  and

synergistic  interactions among  constructs. By addressing these

limitations,  future  studies  can  enhance  the  robustness  and

applicability of research findings in the area of AI adoption among

SMEs.
